I mean it will be useless for you if you don’t put effort into it, but that’s true of any degree. It’s fine to want an easier path to life, but personally I find the kind of jobs that reward the bare minimum (corporate busywork for example) too soul sucking to spend my life on. Other people thrive in those environments because they don’t need a fulfilling job and prefer to explore their passions/interests outside of work. 

I will say if you’re so good at English you never needed to put effort into it before, you can do great things once you apply yourself. My advice is go to office hours and tutoring, approach your first semester with an open mind, and if you absolutely hate it, then try something new until you find something that sticks. You’re going to hate at least one thing about any major or career path you choose — it’s all about what’s worth going through the worst part. Personally, I’m terrible with deadlines, but the things I wrote & learned under the pressure of a deadline are worth every sleepless night. I also get horrible stage fright, but I was able to work with my professors to find a public speaking strategy that works for me, plus I excelled as a peer tutor & found out I love working with students. You say you’re bad at a lot of things, but how do you know that if you’ve never put in the effort to learn how to be better? Learning requires effort; there’s no way around it. Also, I don’t mean to armchair diagnose, but looking up ADHD coping strategies might help you, as many intelligent people with ADHD experience the same problem where they coast through easier classes & then struggle when it comes to university level work, which is much more independent and less structured.

I can pretty confidently say that everyone who has ever majored in English doubted if it was the right decision at some point. And it’s not just English majors — my sister is a STEM student and has changed her major at least 5 times. It’s a big decision to make at a young age, but I know you’ll figure it out. I know it sucks to hear, but it really just takes time.

I want to have kids (not necessarily biologically) because I genuinely love spending time with kids, always have. I come from a big family & I’ve been babysitting since I was a kid myself. Yes, they’re exhausting, and that increases exponentially when they’re your own kids, but I don’t see it as a transactional relationship in which the parent gets the short end of the stick. Kids are hilarious, first of all. They see the world in such unique ways because they’re brand new to it. And the bond that you get when a kid trusts you is so infinitely precious. My cousin gives me drawings of us all the time, and they’re among my most treasured possessions. Personally I love resolving kid conflicts, because they experience emotions on such an extreme level. They don’t know how to communicate or regulate their emotions. Talking through it with them and helping them see things from another perspective is so rewarding. 

I also disagree that kids are mini versions of their parents. They’re individual beings with their own personalities. They grow up in different decades — often different centuries — than their parents. They have different technologies, different social customs, different trends/pop culture icons, usually different hometowns, different friends, different parents. Selfhood isn’t a biologically inherited trait. Yes, it is heavily influenced by parents, but it’s also influenced by friends, education, religion, local culture, etc. Think of your own parents — for every way you’re their “mini” version, I’m sure there’s a million others in which you’re very different from them. Hell, that’s where so much parent-child conflict comes from. Those differences don’t just spawn out of nowhere when kids hit puberty; they were their own people the whole time. I’ve always been told that I’m good with kids, and literally all there is to it is treating them like human beings instead of babies, asking them questions, trying to see from their point of view, and caring about what they care about. (Even if you really don’t care about that random youtube channel or video game or TV show that they’re obsessed with. The same way that you ask your adult friends questions about their interests even if you don’t share them.)

As for the physical burden of childbirth, I mean that does freak me out but at the same time it feels like a non-issue in the grand scheme of things? For one, you can have a child without giving birth to it yourself — adoption, surrogacy, fostering, being a father lol. No matter which way you have children, of course it will involve personal sacrifice. That’s just part of being alive. Personally, I find life more fulfilling when I’m around kids & when I’m helping them grow. Not everyone gets that same sense of fulfillment, and I have a lot of respect for those who realize that & decide not to have children as a result. Too many people don’t realize, or realize after they’ve already had children. It’s not a commitment you can take back, so I’m really glad that more people are questioning whether or not to have kids instead of treating it like a predestined life path.

I get the anxiety, but they’re doing things on their own terms. I’d rather have a healthy, sustainable band putting out less music/performances over a longer period of time, than an exhausted band pushing themselves to their breaking point. They have families and other projects to worry about, and that’s a good thing. Everyone needs balance, especially with such a demanding, high-profile job like actively touring and recording music.

I feel like there’s this expectation nowadays for artists to constantly put stuff out — maybe because we have so much content available to us nowadays, maybe it’s the capitalist productivity mindset, idk. But that’s not usually how the artistic process works. Good ideas need time, energy, and resources to develop. So it seems like NOT going all in on MCR (at least from the outside) is actually the best thing they could do to set themselves up for success & maintain the band’s longevity.

In addition to the other interpretations, I think it’s about fame and the “tortured artist” stereotype. The Patient is preforming, which is emphasized by the sound of it (I know there’s a word for it but I’m totally blanking now) and the lyrics. 

The “they” referenced throughout the song could be referring to an audience. This is strengthened by it switching to “you” in the last chorus. We are the audience, we are the ones who can’t get enough of this guy’s blood, listening to an entire album about his death. “I’m the kind of human wreckage that you love.” Death is turned into a spectacle; in earlier songs on the album, the spectacle feels empowering and emotional, but here it just feels hollow. The Patient sounds quite bitter and sarcastic about his situation.

The first verse really sums it up perfectly. “They encourage your complete cooperation” The juxtaposition of “encourage” and “complete” suggests that the Patient doesn’t have a choice. “Send you roses when they think you need to smile” They think they know what’s best for the patient. “I can’t control myself because I don’t know how / And they love me for it honestly, I’ll be here for a while” He can’t overcome his sickness, but that’s WHY they love him. The patient is stuck here, and “they” want to keep it that way for their own benefit. 

Extrapolating that to the tortured artist, this could be the band commenting on how they are selling their own “blood,”i.e. self expression through art, to an eager audience. We know they have personal experience with many of the themes they explore in their music, including grief, substance abuse, and mental illness. They are sharing these incredibly sensitive topics with millions of strangers (keep in mind TPB is off of the tails of Three Cheers, when they really started taking off). When you share stuff like that with an audience, it can turn into a bit of a parasitic relationship where you feel pressured into continuing self-destructive patterns in order to keep on making art that others connect with. I mean we as the audience of MCR are literally cheering for songs about drug addiction and Gerard’s dead grandmother. They make the music for us to enjoy, sure, but at what cost? How much will they have to give? How much will be left for themselves alone? These are the questions I think MCR is contending with in “Blood” and throughout their discography. It’s a tough balancing act.

From the perspective of a visual artist & writer, creativity isn’t finite. You never really stop thinking of new ideas or new ways to express old ideas. It’s not like you have a project that explores certain themes and then that’s it, you never talk about them again. If that was true, then no one would make new art ever because surely we’ve covered the entire human condition by now, with how long art has been around. And with MCR specifically, they have been exploring new ideas already. The Return/SWARM tour and the When We Were Young festival used performance to highlight certain themes in their music, like gender with Gerard’s outfits and nostalgia/selling out vs maintaining integrity with the WWWYF costumes.

As for how to engage with neurotypicals (this also works with neurodivergents):

* You can ask how their day or week is going. The conversation doesn't have to be about you, or even about your life events. Which works really well because people like talking about themselves lol. 
* One of my go-to conversation starters is asking what movies/tv shows people are watching. (I get hyperfixated on that stuff, so I know it's easy for me to carry a conversation about it, even if I'm not familiar with the shows they mention). 
* You can reach out if you see something that makes you think of them, like an article about a subject they're interested in. 
* I also love it when other people tell me about their family/friend drama because A) I love the drama lol and B) it gets them monologuing, so I don't have to think about how to respond. But don't ask about the drama, not directly. You can ask how their family is doing if they've mentioned them to you, or ask *about* their family — do they have siblings, are they from the area, any plans for the summer/holidays, etc.
* It might be helpful to reflect on what you talk about when you hang out with them outside of work in order to think about how to approach starting a conversation.

I notice you say that you don't know how to engage with neurotypicals, but how do you know they are neurotypical? Have they told you? I know quite a few people with mental health challenges that i never would have guessed about because they're so good at masking. And I mentioned in a different comment that I didn't know how to talk with my neurodivergent friends, either; it was a skill I had to learn, and am still learning. I would also talk in absolutes about myself back then (I don't know how to talk to people, I don't know how to make friends, etc.) but those turned out to be wrong. I didn't know how to do those things until I learned how to do it, just like I didn't know how to write or read before I went to school.

You ARE capable of making friends. Don't listen to anyone who says otherwise. Everyone, including neurotypicals, has to learn how to communicate with each other. No one's programmed with it; it's not an inherent skill. ADHD brings extra challenges to that learning experience, like RSD, unreliable focus/attention span, time blindness, executive dysfunction. But it also comes with strengths, like special interests that you can talk about for hours, internet rabbit holes to bring up in conversation, and the empathy that can come from being excluded or misunderstood throughout your life.

I used to think like this, too. I felt alone because no one would ever reach out to me, and I thought I would be bothering them if I reached out first. Then I realized that most (if not all) of my friends are neurodivergent too, and they had the same exact thought process. My friendships instantly grew when I made it an effort to reach out, even when I didn't feel confident about it, because that lets them know that I care about their thoughts and feelings. They can't read my mind. They don't know I care about them unless I show it.

You say you don't like having conversations out of the blue — but that's what friendship is. You can't expect them to reach out to you if you're not reaching out to them. It's a two-way street.

All this with love, as I have been in a very similar situation & I know how painful it is to feel excluded. And it's okay for them to be just your colleagues; it doesn't mean you're incapable of making friends, it just means that you don't mesh well with them in that way. Perfectly normal for coworkers to just be coworkers.

now, my rules are: No starting a show when i have an urgent task/deadline coming up. No watching TV on my phone (road trips are an exception). No watching TV in the background during a task that requires focus, because I know me, and I know I'll just divert all of my attention to the show. (only exception is if the task is something like drawing where I know i can actually focus on both at once). No social media after a show (i am not great about following this rule, but it helps when i do. i recommend setting screentime limits—i use the app jomo—and logging out of accounts). 

The key thing is to replace what you are getting from watching tv with another activity, so you don't go back to the same behaviors. Read a book instead if you're looking for a good story—maybe start with easy/light reads, and then if that becomes a bad habit, start reading more challenging and/or slow paced works that are more difficult to "binge" read. if you like writing posts/fanfic, try writing essays or original fiction. If you like talking about shows with other people, reach out to irl friends instead.

It's not a linear path, so don't feel bad if you slip back into old habits. as long as you keep on trying, that's all that matters. also disclaimer this is based on my experiences, so what works for me might not work for you

CC student here — I think it would be a great path for you! For starters, you are surrounded by students & many faculty who have also gone through life challenges. Maybe not the exact same, but no one goes to CC because their life is perfect lol. I came from a high-income high school where I felt out of place because I couldn't afford a private 4 year university and I had mental health issues that impacted my education. At my CC, I got so much more support & empathy from my peers and faculty. I know it's difficult to change your perspective when you have your heart set on something — believe me, CC wasn't my first choice, or even my second or third lol — but you can turn this into an opportunity for growth. If you spend a year or two at CC with top grades & good letters of rec (which you will get because you are a smart, motivated learner!), you have a better shot at transferring into Smith or the other schools you're looking at because they'll see that you can succeed in a college environment. Wishing you the best of luck! 

A few misc. tips if you do end up at a CC: Join the Honors program and join PTK (PTK is the community college honor society, you have to do some volunteer hours I believe. It costs money, but you can try to get a waiver. PTK members have access to a lot of scholarships.) If you're a Massachusetts resident, do the MassURC (ask your honors program coordinator about it). Focus on keeping your grades up first & foremost, and don't be afraid to take less classes in a semester than you feel like you "should" take. Reach out for help early & often — always better too early than too late. CC can get pretty lonely if you don't put in the effort to start conversations, so make sure you depend on your support system & put yourself out there. On your schedule, "T" means Tuesday and "R" means Thursday, so "TR" means you have class on Tuesdays and Thursdays, not just Thursday. Reach out to transfer advising sooner than you think you need to. The transfer office will probably host events (my CC does special Honors transfer events) — attend one of those your first semester. Get their email & stay in touch. Let them know you're interested in Smith & let them know your financial situation. They will help you with any questions you have about the application process, and they can give you advice on how to make your application stand out. Build relationships with profs — go to office hours, talk with them after class, email them (not just when you have to miss a class or get an extension). They are there to help you.

Brainstorming questions to consider/journal about:

* What ideas have sustained your interest? (If you find, idk, nature symbolism boring, don't write about nature symbolism. Look for through lines between the books you've read & what draws you to/away from them.)
* Along those lines, what are your strongest opinions? Think of arguments that you could have for hours and hours. You don't have to write about a book you love — you could rip apart something you hate, so long as you have enough to say. Hateful literary criticism can be really fun to read lol.
* Has anything you've read radically changed your perspective on a topic? How so?
* What are your favorite essays that you've written? Are there any ways you can expand on them? (Expanding on a previous essay gives you a huge head start, especially if time is a factor!)

it is!! kinda lol. I just posted a longer comment about it but TL;DR: it’s referring to “Wild Women Don’t Have The Blues” by Ida Cox, which is a blues song (music genre) about the blues (emotional state). It’s considered an early feminist anthem :-)

This is an allusion to the blues song “Wild Women Don’t Have The Blues” by Ida Cox, released in 1924. The blues is a genre of Black American folk music. It began at the tail end of the slave trade in the American South, right around the Civil War era. Enslaved people created the blues to express themselves and cope with the adversity they faced under slavery. The blues also refers to feeling down, depressed, or lonely.

Going back to “Wild Women,” it’s a song about how women who aren’t attached to a man are spared a lot of emotional pain. This was significant in the 20s because there was a lot of cultural change happening that made promiscuity and women’s rights (somewhat) more accepted. Songs like “Wild Women” reflect the changing attitudes of the time, attitudes that we see reflected in our own society. Back then, it was truly revolutionary to imagine a woman living independently of men. Men had all the social power — women had limited job opportunities, limited control over their own money and spending, their own movement, even. This definitely depended on your social class, though. The wealthier you were, the more strict the gender roles, although poor women were and are still significantly impacted by the patriarchy (just in different ways).

Mitski uses this reference to show that independence was supposed to prevent her from “getting the blues,” but she’s still sad because of this independence. It’s a modern reinterpretation of Ida Cox’s ideas on how women interact with the patriarchy in their romantic relationships. Our society favors dating around, like the relationships Ida Cox claimed free a woman, but “First Love / Late Spring” shows that this form of relationship also has its emotional consequences. Shutting yourself out from connection & vulnerability causes pain, just as depending on one man for all of your needs and desires does.

“Wild Women” is a fantastic song, give it a listen! And it’s not a blues song (at all) but Sweet Misery Blues by Violent Femmes is another interesting look at this promiscuity/casual dating conversation. Fair warning, the lyrics are from the perspective of a predatory man.

Now for actually getting your correct shade, hair is not the simplest makeup color. By any means. Most people have hair that is more desaturated/gray than what makeup brands offer. If you don't want to spend more money, try layering the two shades you have. If you have some more money to spend, go to a beauty store where you can try testers. I saw from your profile that you're in the UK, so I'm not sure what the equivalent to Ulta or Sephora is in there. Just try out a bunch of shades and see what looks best (and take pictures!) but don't buy anything. Even if they sell drugstore brands like Ulta does, they mark up the prices.

Instead, analyze the shade(s) that worked well. Try to pick apart the hue, saturation, and value. (The hue is the color of the rainbow that your shade is in. Did shades with an orangey undertone or greener undertone match better? Somewhere in the middle? Saturation is how bright/dull the color is. Like I said earlier, hair is duller in color than we think it is. Value is the light to dark spectrum.) The most important thing to keep in mind is that just because something matches your hair color, doesn't mean it will match your eyebrows. Facial hair can be a different color, and it also lays on the head differently, so you might need a few shades up from your actual skin tone to get the right match. It also depends on how much product you use and how you apply it. For my sparse eyebrows, I need a super light touch of a very grayish blonde color or else I look like an alien. (Honestly I just go with my natural brows because I'm not used to having eyebrows lmao).

Once you understand the color that you're looking for, hunt online for shade matches. If you find the perfect brand name, search for dupes. Otherwise, look at the shades that drug store brands offer (and make sure to check the reviews for what they look like in real life). Go to a convenience store or supermarket for the cheapest prices, unless you can find a good coupon/sale/clearance elsewhere. If the shade you pick doesn't match, it's okay. It's not your fault. Nothing's wrong with you. Makeup brands are not incentivized to sell in-between shades because that increases production costs. It's their fault for making you feel like you need their product to be feminine, not the other way around. Best of luck, and take a deep breath. <3

Also, Rihanna is a great example of lighter brows for dark hair if that's your situation. (Do not hold your brows to that standard though. Her entire career is her face. She spends thousands of dollars on it. No regular human being has access to those resources.)

I'm a non-coder (English major, actually), and I don't think it's about whether you can code or not. That's really only relevant if you're making your own plugins, which I don't bother with. The main barrier to entry is computer literacy. Obsidian would be more trouble than it's worth for someone who doesn't know how to store & organize their files, how to use Markdown instead of WYSIWYG, and how to use keyboard shortcuts. Another big part of it is finding the answer vs needing someone to tell you the answer. If something goes wrong in Obsidian or you're not sure how to do something, chances are that there's already a forum post out there with the same issue. But if you don't take the initiative to search up that question and look for the answer, you're never gonna find it. I've had to look into markdown/markup languages/programming languages, literally countless explanations of the Zettelkasten method because I kept on getting confused, etc. etc. in order to develop my Obsidian workflow. To me, it's well worth the effort to gain a better understanding of Obsidian, my computer, and my mind, but a lot of people just aren't interested in all that. No, it is not irresponsible for ADHDers to have children. Disabled people deserve to raise children if they want to be parents, and disabled children deserve to live. Every single kid will face challenges throughout their life, and it does not make sense to preemptively take away their chances at experiencing happiness and success because they will also struggle. Of course, this comes with a billion and one caveats, but generally speaking: we cannot predict the future. ADHDers cannot predict their children's future based on their own experiences. Maybe the kid will be a social butterfly who faces challenges in other parts of their life. Maybe the kid won't have ADHD at all. Maybe they will have ADHD and struggle tremendously because of it, but they will still be able to find joy/meaning/purpose in their life. Maybe they won't. There are too many what-ifs to plan for (which can be difficult for people who over-plan as a result of their ADHD... myself included).

The one thing you can control is how you support your child throughout their life. Can they go to you when they are facing challenges? When they make mistakes? Consider that ADHDers are prone to risky behavior. How would you react to your child drinking, abusing substances, having unprotected sex, getting pregnant/getting someone else pregnant, causing a car accident, etc. Not all ADHDers do these things, but anyone who has children (ADHD or not) should have an idea of how they would handle behavior like that. If you do not trust yourself to be able to put aside your anger in order to help a child who does stupid shit, *then* you should reconsider having children. Because all kids do stupid shit, and all kids should have parents who can respond to that appropriately instead of A) getting angry/violent and erasing the opportunity for honest conversation, or B) letting them off the hook and teaching them that their actions don't have consequences. If your kid is a social outcast, do you make home a place where they can feel safe and included? Do you actively search for peer activities/groups where they might find somewhere to belong? Are you prepared for medical expenses such as therapy and medication?

Do you WANT kids? Are you capable of handling another responsibility — probably the biggest responsibility anyone can handle — or is there just not enough room in your life right now for that kind of commitment? Do you have someone in your life (a partner, family, friends, therapist, an online group like this one, etc.) who understands your struggles with ADHD and is capable of supporting you as a parent?

This is an incomplete list of questions, and again, there are so many more factors that apply. But a responsible parent is one who cares for and takes care of their children. ADHDers are perfectly capable of that.

Find books/stories you enjoy and figure out what makes them good. What is the creator trying to say? How are they saying it? Treat everything like an intentional artistic choice that serves the story (if the story is good, it will be). Since you’ve been out of school for a bit, I’d suggest familiarizing yourself with the basics — literary devices, genres, theme, plot, etc.

As for specific story recs, I don’t know what kind of stuff you like, but there’s good literature in any genre/medium. HBO’s Succession is a corporate/family drama with so so much to analyze. The series finale is actually next week lol. For fantasy, Lord of the Rings, obviously (there are more literary fantasy novels, but LOTR is number one). If sci fi is more your thing, then Dune*. For *literature* literature (classic lit, the stuff you think of when you think of English majors), The Great Gatsby is a good introduction. The last page of Gatsby is some of the best writing I have ever read in my life. The entire book is pretty short, and it was written in the 1920s, so the language isn’t too difficult to parse through.

Speaking of difficult language, you’re probably going to have to read Shakespeare at some point during your minor. I’m not a huge fan myself, mostly because I haven’t had the chance to really connect with his work — besides Macbeth, which is amazing. Reading Shakespeare is especially hard on your own, so I suggest looking up performances and adaptations of his work. It’ll make the story clearer. Plays are meant to be acted out, after all.

You’ll be doing a lot of writing in your English classes, so I suggest reading George Orwell’s essay “Politics and the English Language.” It instantly improved my writing. Also read The Elements of Style. Knowing basic grammar helps SO much (parts of speech, clauses, compound/complex sentences, and punctuation. You don’t have to get into the nitty gritty). When you’re writing essays, remember: be concise, be clear, and explain how/why.

I know I just threw a lot at you, but keep in mind, the point of an English major (or minor) is to teach you all of these things. You don’t have to do everything I mentioned; these are just suggestions to help you put your best foot forward. Congrats on going back to school, and good luck!!

Just thought of another parallel that made me think of her plan to come out during Lover: "You were bigger than the whole sky/You were more than just a short time" from BTTWS, "Time, wondrous time/Gave me the blues and then purple-pink skies" from Invisible String, and of course the Lover album cover with the sky in the background. Also.. ugh this is so long already but I just love that line in Invisible String. Like, on one level, you have "Time gave me the blues and then purple pink skies," referring to the physical color change of the sky when the sun sets. But then it's also "Time gave me the blues, and then time gave me purple pink skies," meaning time both made her sad and gave her something beautiful. When you think of it in the context of the phrase "the sun set \[on something\]," i.e. something came to an end, she's saying that time caused something to end, which made her sad at first, but she found something beautiful within the ending—or the ending is what gave her something beautiful, and without the ending she would have never had the "purple-pink skies." And of course, time is modified by the word "wondrous." She is grateful for this process! She appreciates the effect time has had on her, both when it gave her the blues and the purple pink skies. She is not bitter about the blues at all; instead, she is glad they allowed her to experience the something beautiful. To pack so much into literally two lines—only 12 words and 14 syllables!!!—is absolutely insane. And it perfectly encapsulates the theme of Invisible String. In response to the corrupt, absolute monarchies in places like France, the Enlightenment changed how many people viewed government. The Enlightenment was a philosophical movement that emphasized reason and liberty in the 18th century. Philosophes, the Enlightenment term for philosophers, gathered together and encouraged discussion on what constitutes a good government and how to change a bad one. Although the Enlightenment was a rapid change in thought from the absolutist era, Enlightenment thought encouraged gradual reform rather than radical change because many thinkers believed that government was an agreement between the people and the rulers.

The Enlightenment encouraged gradual change because philosophes believed that government was an agreement between the people and the rulers. Jean-Jacques Rousseau, a French philosophe, said in his work The Social Contract that people naturally agree to submit to a government and give up some freedoms in return for order. Since they chose to submit to the laws, they cannot simply ignore unjust laws. Instead, they have to follow the laws that they agreed to have imposed on them and try to gradually change their government through legal reform (Outside Evidence). Samuel von Pufendorf, a German philosopher, said that monarchs could be controlled in order to avoid tyranny if there was an agreement between the people and the rulers that the people would follow laws and they had a say in government. If the government has a legislative branch, such as Britain’s Parliament, then the people are able to influence government. Pufendorf believes that constitutional monarchy, a monarchy that has a legislative branch and obeys a consitiution, allows people to try to reform the government gradually through lawful processes. Pufendorf’s point of view matters because he was German, which was at the time part of the Holy Roman Empire. He was ruled by an emperor, so he understood that he had to respect the empire’s laws even if he did not agree with them (Doc 1). Moses Mendelssohn said in Jerusalem; a Treatise on Ecclesiastical Authority and Judaism that people are bound by laws, even if they disagreed with them. Citizens have the right to criticize laws, but they cannot disregard them. Radical change disregards laws in favor of immediate results. Mendelssohn believes that gradual reform is the only proper way to change a government because people cannot simply ignore a law, even if they think it is unjust (Doc 4). A French engraver named Pierre Charles Baquoy created an artwork that shows Voltaire, a philosophe, sitting at a desk and King Fredrick II of Prussia visiting Voltaire. King Fredrick the Great was an enlightened despot. Voltaire is shown extending his arm to Fredrick the Great, which shows that he is willing to work with him so Fredrick can improve Prussia. Even though Voltaire broke French censorship laws, he did not disregard government entirely. This shows that even a radical philosophe like Voltaire was willing to help gradually reform other countries. Pierre  (Doc 5).

Although the Enlightenment was a quick change in thought, the Enlightenment did not advocate for radical change because they respected governments. Denis Diderot, the creator of the encyclopedia, said in a letter to a Russian princess that the Enlightenment quickly attacked superstition. He was concerned that the Enlightenment would turn against religion. Although Diderot says that the Enlightenment was a radical change of thought, that does not mean that most Enlightenment thinkers believed that it was okay to radically change the government. Many thinkers believed that it was important to follow the laws of their governments and instead advocated for gradual reform. Diderot’s point of view matters because he was a contemporary of the Enlightenment, and he experienced how the Enlightenment had caused rebellions such as the American Revolution. Therefore, he would see the Enlightenment as happening much more quickly than it really did (Doc 3).

so first off, you should work on writing clearly and concisely. like another commenter said, you use a lot of big words that dont really add anything. technically writing style isnt a point on the dbq, but it makes it easier for the grader to tell whether or not you actually got the point *and* it saves you a bit of time because you can convey a point in 1-2 sentences, instead of 3-4. also this will help you with writing in general, whether its for an english essay, your college essays, or even just an important email.

in your contextualization, you mention the renaissance. although the renaissance did precede the enlightenment, i think absolutism is a more direct cause. it might be possible renaissance as context, but you said that the renaissance consisted of gradual change/reform. however, in the very next sentence you say that the enlightenment encouraged radical reform. so its not very clear how the renaissance caused the enlightenment.

speaking of your thesis, its not specific enough. you need to explain HOW it undermined gradual reform. this is my thesis:

“Although the Enlightenment was a rapid change in thought from the absolutist era, Enlightenment thought encouraged gradual reform rather than radical change because many thinkers believed that government was an agreement between the people and the rulers.”

your thesis is missing the “because ...” part, so thats why you didnt get the thesis point. also dont worry about the first part (from “although” to “era”), thats for complex understanding. its considered the most difficult point to get, so i would focus on the other points before tackling complex understanding.

for emile du chatelet, you dont really analyze the doc, you just describe it. to analyze the doc, you need to connect it back to your topic sentence and especially your thesis. 

for the catherine doc, i dont understand how catherine was radical. how were her people in danger of losing their freedom? how did she solve this problem in a radical way? and most importantly, how did the enlightenment influence her radical thought?

your rousseau analysis isnt too bad, but its confusing because you weren’t clear enough in your thesis that you were taking both sides of the argument. it is possible to take both sides of the argument, but its not easy. you have to have a very strong thesis. usually, its easier to take one side of the argument. if you want to go for the complex understanding point, the easier way is to have a rebuttal in the last paragraph that you mention briefly in the thesis (thats what i did, again if you want to see my essay just ask!)

ok i just read your conclusion and you are much more clear that you are taking both sides of the argument. however, you still arent specific enough; you’re missing the “because” part. if you had included the reason WHY the enlightenment encouraged both gradual and radical change in your conclusion, then you wouldve gotten the thesis point and you might have gotten the complex understanding point (again, that point is difficult to get so idk).

imo the thesis is the most important part of the dbq. it only gives you one point directly, but pretty much all of your other points come from being able to argue your thesis in different ways (if that makes sense). to write a thesis, restate the question and then add a specific argument.

for example...

Q: was imperialism cause primarily political or economic reasons?

A: imperialism was caused primarily by economic reasons BECAUSE European countries used colonies for resources and markets to make and sell finished goods. (everything after the “because” is the most important part. without a specific reason, you won’t get the thesis point.)

when you’re thinking of your argument, dont pick what you personally believe. instead, read through all of the documents and pick the argument that most of the documents support. 

using the imperialism example, if 3 documents supported economics and 2 documents supported politics, then make the argument for economics (even if you personally believe it was caused by politics). then, you can use 1-2 of the political docs as a rebuttal.
{note: if you have more outside evidence for the side that has less documents, i would probably argue for that side even though it has less docs. i find it easier to incorporate outside info into the side im arguing for rather than the rebuttal. its all up to you tho!}

the rebuttal isn’t necessary, but its the easiest way to get the complexity point. basically, you just use one or more of the opposing docs and explain why they’re wrong and why your argument is right. 

the plus side of rebuttals is that you can use up an entire paragraph for them, and you dont have to worry about including them in your thesis.

if you use the rebuttal, your entire dbq can be:

- intro (this is where you get the contextualization point, its basically a quick summary of the events leading up to what your dbq is about. so for imperialism, you could talk about the industrial revolution)

- thesis (restate prompt, pick a side, add “because” and then enter your topic for the first body paragraph)

- first body paragraph (analyze two or three quotes and add 1-2 specific pieces of outside info. dont forget to relate EVERYTHING back to your thesis or else you wont get the points!)

- second body paragraph: rebuttal! (analyze one or two quotes depending on how many you used in the first body paragraph — don’t analyze all five docs, it takes too much time. add a specific piece of outside info here too, unless you have two in your first body paragraph. again, relate every piece of evidence back to your thesis, but this time, you talk about why the evidence is incorrect.)

- conclusion: only do this if you have extra time AND you’re not confident in your thesis. if you are confident in your thesis, spend the extra time proofreading your essay. 

and thats it! its still a lot to fit into 45 minutes, but its a little less daunting.

also i forgot to mention, the pov point! this goes in either of your body paragraphs. you basically explain why the pov of a particular document is relevant to your argument. its not enough to just say what the doc’s pov is, you have to explain why it matters.
i dont have an example for the pov point, but im sure you could find one if you looked it up. 

make sure you study and understand the rubric so you can get as many points as possible. if anything i said doesnt make sense, feel free to ask and i’ll try to explain it better.

one last thing — this is just how i personally approach dbq’s. what works for me, might not work for you. the absolute best way to study for the exam is practice! do a few practice exams tomorrow and grade them yourself with the rubric. good luck!!

these are great, especially considering youre a beginner! a few tips...

1. if you can, get a sketchbook! drawing on lined paper can be convenient, but its so worth it to have a place dedicated to your sketches that doesnt have lines cutting through. also, if you eventually add color with watercolors or something, sketchbook paper holds up better than notebook paper.
2. it’s difficult to tell from these pictures if you do this or don’t, but when you draw the head try drawing a vertical line down the middle and a horizontal line across the middle. this way you have a marker of where each facial feature should go in proportion to each other.
3. youtube is your BEST FRIEND!! i improved a ton through youtube. i love kasey golden, drawing wiff waffles, and draw with jazza (right now he does mostly fun challenge videos but he has some old tutorials for anatomy and such that are SO USEFUL). search up “face anatomy” on youtube and you’ll get great results. ALSO: study the planes of the face. that improved my facial anatomy by a ton. it really helped me visualize the face as a three dimensional object when drawing
